sets.title: Seeds on the move
sets.summary: Students read an informational science text about how seeds travel and practice finding facts, the main idea and supporting evidence.

passage.title: How Seeds Travel
paragraphs: Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can still go on a trip. A seed needs space, sun and water to grow. If every seed fell right under its parent plant, the young plants would be too crowded. So seeds have different ways to travel.
Some seeds travel with the wind. A dandelion seed has soft white hairs. The hairs work like a tiny parachute. The wind lifts the seed and carries it far away.

Other seeds travel with animals. Some seeds have little hooks. The hooks stick to the fur of a dog or a rabbit. Later, the seed falls off in a new place. Birds also help. They eat berries, and the seeds inside drop to the ground far from the bush.
Some seeds travel on water. A coconut is a very big seed. It can float in the ocean for many weeks. When it lands on a beach, it can grow into a new tree.

items.stem: What carries a dandelion seed far away?

visual.alt: A dandelion plant and a seed

choices.text: rain
choices.why: The passage does not say rain moves dandelion seeds.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

choices.text: wind
choices.why: Paragraph 2 says the wind lifts the seed and carries it far away.

choices.text: water
choices.why: Water moves a different seed, not the dandelion seed.
choices.misconception: Uses a detail from the wrong paragraph

items.stem: What can a coconut do in the ocean?

choices.text: It sinks to the bottom.
choices.why: The passage says the opposite of this.
choices.misconception: Reverses the stated fact

choices.text: It flies in the wind.
choices.why: Flying in the wind is how a different seed travels.
choices.misconception: Uses a detail from the wrong paragraph

choices.text: It floats for many weeks.
choices.why: Paragraph 4 says a coconut can float in the ocean for many weeks.

items.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?

choices.text: Dandelion seeds have soft white hairs that catch wind.
choices.why: This is true, but it is only one small detail.
choices.misconception: Chooses a main idea that is too narrow

choices.text: Plants need sun and water to grow big and strong.
choices.why: This is true, but the passage is mostly about how seeds move.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not answer the question

choices.text: Birds like to eat the berries that grow on bushes.
choices.why: Berries are one example, not what the whole passage is about.
choices.misconception: Chooses a main idea that is too narrow

choices.text: Seeds travel in different ways to find space to grow.
choices.why: Every paragraph tells a way seeds travel to a new place to grow.

items.stem: Paragraph 2 says the hairs "work like a tiny parachute." What does this tell you?

choices.text: The hairs help the seed float down slowly.
choices.why: A parachute helps something fall slowly, so the hairs keep the seed in the air.

choices.text: The seed is a real parachute made of cloth.
choices.why: The author compares the hairs to a parachute; the seed is not really cloth.
choices.misconception: Reads figurative language literally

choices.text: The hairs make the seed heavy so it drops fast.
choices.why: A heavy seed would fall fast, not ride on the wind.
choices.misconception: Reverses the meaning of the comparison

choices.text: A person must open the seed so it can fly.
choices.why: The passage never says a person helps the seed.
choices.misconception: Adds outside knowledge that is not in the text

items.stem: A seed has many small hooks. Which animal would most likely carry it to a new place?

choices.text: A fish swimming in a lake
choices.why: A fish has no fur for the hooks to stick to.
choices.misconception: Ignores the key detail that hooks stick to fur

choices.text: A bird that eats berries
choices.why: Birds help seeds that are inside berries, not seeds with hooks.
choices.misconception: Mixes up two different ways seeds travel

choices.text: A dog with thick fur
choices.why: The passage says hooks stick to fur, so a furry dog could carry the seed.

choices.text: A turtle with a smooth shell
choices.why: Hooks need fur to hold on to, and a smooth shell has none.
choices.misconception: Ignores the key detail in the text

items.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that seeds need to move away from their parent plant?

choices.text: "A dandelion seed has soft white hairs."
choices.why: This tells what a seed looks like, not why it needs to move.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not support the claim

choices.text: "If every seed fell right under its parent plant, the young plants would be too crowded."
choices.why: This sentence gives the reason seeds need to go somewhere new.

choices.text: "Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can still go on a trip."
choices.why: This tells that seeds travel, but not why they need to move away.
choices.misconception: Chooses evidence that shows that, not why

choices.text: "The hooks stick to the fur of a dog or a rabbit."
choices.why: This tells how some seeds move, but not why seeds need to move.
choices.misconception: Chooses evidence that shows how, not why

sets.title: Lina and the quiet drum
sets.summary: Students read an original short story and practice finding details, putting events in order and understanding figurative language and character feelings.

passage.title: The Quiet Drum
paragraphs: Lina had a small drum from her grandmother. Every morning she tapped it softly on the porch. Tap, tap, tap. The sound was like rain on a roof.
One day, the class planned a music show. Mr. Osei asked, "Who wants to play an instrument?" Lina's hands felt cold. Her heart was a jumping frog. She wanted to play, but she was nervous.
At home, Lina told her grandmother about the show. Grandmother smiled. "Play the song you play every morning," she said. "Close your eyes and think of the porch."

On the day of the show, Lina sat on a chair in front of everyone. She closed her eyes. She tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Soon her classmates clapped along with her beat. When she opened her eyes, everyone was smiling.
After the show, Lina ran to her grandmother. "They liked the rain song!" she said. Grandmother hugged her. "The drum was never quiet," she said. "It was waiting for you."

glossary.esDefinition: la parte abierta con techo enfrente de una casa

glossary.definition: a thing you use to make music
glossary.esDefinition: una cosa que usas para hacer música

glossary.definition: the other students in your class
glossary.esDefinition: los otros estudiantes de tu clase

glossary.esDefinition: el sonido constante de la música que puedes seguir con aplausos

items.stem: What did Lina get from her grandmother?

choices.text: a book
choices.why: The story does not say Lina got a book.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

choices.text: a ball
choices.why: A ball is not in the story.
choices.misconception: Guesses a common object from outside the text

choices.text: a drum
choices.why: The first sentence says Lina had a small drum from her grandmother.

items.stem: Where did Lina play her drum every morning?

choices.text: on the porch
choices.why: Paragraph 1 says she tapped it softly on the porch every morning.

choices.text: at school
choices.why: She played at school only on the day of the show, not every morning.
choices.misconception: Mixes up two different times in the story

choices.text: at the park
choices.why: The story never talks about a park.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

items.stem: What did Grandmother do right after Lina told her about the show?

choices.text: She gave Lina a big hug.
choices.why: The hug happens at the end, after the show is over.
choices.misconception: Puts events in the wrong order

choices.text: She told Lina which song to play.
choices.why: Paragraph 3 says Grandmother smiled and told Lina to play her morning song.

choices.text: She clapped along with the beat.
choices.why: The classmates clapped, not Grandmother.
choices.misconception: Gives an action to the wrong character

choices.text: She bought Lina a new drum.
choices.why: The story never says Grandmother bought a drum.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

items.stem: The story says, "Her heart was a jumping frog." What does this mean?

choices.text: Lina had a pet frog that lived at home.
choices.why: There is no real frog; the author is comparing her heart to a frog.
choices.misconception: Reads figurative language literally

choices.text: Lina liked to jump and play like a frog.
choices.why: The sentence is about how her heart felt, not about a game.
choices.misconception: Focuses on one word and misses the meaning

choices.text: Lina felt calm and happy about the show.
choices.why: Her cold hands show she did not feel calm.
choices.misconception: Chooses the opposite feeling

choices.text: Her heart beat fast because she was nervous.
choices.why: A jumping frog moves fast, like a heart that beats fast when you are nervous.

items.stem: Why did Grandmother tell Lina to think of the porch?

choices.text: So Lina would feel calm, like she did at home
choices.why: The porch was where Lina played every day, so thinking of it could help her relax.

choices.text: Because the music show was going to be on the porch
choices.why: The show was in front of the class, not on the porch.
choices.misconception: Confuses the setting of two events

choices.text: So Lina would forget the song she played
choices.why: Grandmother wanted Lina to play the song, not forget it.
choices.misconception: Reverses the character's purpose

choices.text: Because Grandmother wanted to go back home
choices.why: The story does not say this, and they were already at home.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

items.stem: Grandmother says, "The drum was never quiet. It was waiting for you." What does she mean?

choices.text: The drum was broken until the day of the show.
choices.why: Nothing in the story says the drum was broken.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

choices.text: The drum makes loud sounds all day long.
choices.why: Lina tapped it softly, and Grandmother is not talking about how loud it is.
choices.misconception: Reads figurative language literally

choices.text: The music was there; Lina just had to be brave.
choices.why: Grandmother means the drum was ready, and now Lina was ready to play for others.

choices.text: Lina should wait a long time to play again.
choices.why: Grandmother is proud of Lina, not telling her to wait.
choices.misconception: Misreads the character's message

sets.title: Counting our class books
sets.summary: Students read a short math explanation with a data table and practice reading the table, following steps to add and using numbers as evidence.

passage.title: The Book Chart
paragraphs: Room 8 has a reading goal. The class wants to read 50 books in four weeks. Each Friday, a student helper counts the books on the class list. Then the helper writes the number in a table.
Here are the numbers. In Week 1, the class read 12 books. In Week 2, they read 15 books. In Week 3, many students were sick, so the class read only 9 books. In Week 4, they read 18 books.
To find the total, Ms. Rahman showed the class how to add. First, add 12 and 15 to get 27. Next, add 9 to get 36. Last, add 18. The total is 54 books.
Did the class meet the goal? Yes! The goal was 50 books, and they read 54. That is 4 more books than the goal. The class celebrated with a picnic in the park.

18 is the number for Week 4.

items.stem: What does the student helper count each Friday?

choices.text: pencils
choices.why: The passage does not talk about counting pencils.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

choices.text: students
choices.why: Students are in the passage, but the helper does not count them.
choices.misconception: Picks a word from the text that does not answer the question

choices.text: books
choices.why: Paragraph 1 says the helper counts the books on the class list.

items.stem: Why did the class read only 9 books in Week 3?

choices.text: Many students were sick.
choices.why: Paragraph 2 says many students were sick, so they read fewer books.

choices.text: The class went on a picnic.
choices.why: The picnic happened at the end, after they met the goal.
choices.misconception: Puts a later event in the wrong place

choices.text: The goal was too big.
choices.why: The class met the goal, and the passage does not say it was too big.
choices.misconception: Adds an opinion that is not in the text

choices.text: The helper forgot to count.
choices.why: The passage never says the helper forgot.
choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

items.stem: Ms. Rahman added 12 and 15 first. Which number did she add next?

choices.why: 18 is added last, not next.
choices.misconception: Skips a step in the sequence

choices.why: 27 is the answer to the first step, not the next number to add.
choices.misconception: Confuses a result with a step

choices.why: 54 is the total at the very end.
choices.misconception: Jumps to the final answer

choices.why: Paragraph 3 says, "Next, add 9."

items.stem: How many more books did the class read in Week 4 than in Week 1?

choices.text: 30 more books
choices.why: This adds the two weeks, but the question asks how many more.
choices.misconception: Adds when the question asks for a difference

choices.text: 6 more books
choices.why: Week 4 had 18 books and Week 1 had 12, and 18 minus 12 is 6.

choices.text: 3 more books
choices.why: This compares Week 4 with Week 2, not Week 1.
choices.misconception: Uses numbers from the wrong row

choices.text: 4 more books
choices.why: 4 is how many more than the goal, not the difference between the weeks.
choices.misconception: Uses a number from the text that answers a different question

items.stem: Jamal says, "Our class met its goal." Which detail best supports what Jamal says?

choices.text: The class read 54 books, and the goal was 50.
choices.why: 54 is more than 50, so this proves the class met the goal.

choices.text: The class read 18 books in Week 4.
choices.why: This is one week only, so it does not show the whole goal was met.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not prove the claim

choices.text: A helper counts the books each Friday.
choices.why: This tells how they counted, not if they met the goal.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not prove the claim

choices.text: Many students were sick in Week 3.
choices.why: This tells about a hard week, not about meeting the goal.
choices.misconception: Chooses evidence that does not connect to the claim
